source_caption:
The iconic battlefield sequence in 1917 (2019), where Lance Corporal Schofield runs parallel to the trench as a mass of British troops charges over the top, remains one of the most remarkable cinematic sequences of the decade.

What makes the scene extraordinary is not simply what happens in front of the camera, but how it was captured. Schofield’s roughly one-minute battlefield sprint was filmed as a single continuous long take, with George MacKay actually running around 300 metres while more than 500 extras, explosions and meticulously choreographed action unfolded around him. The camera had to move with him throughout the run, requiring an elaborate combination of camera rigs, vehicles and precisely timed choreography. Every movement had to be rehearsed and synchronized down to the smallest detail. 

Much of that visual ingenuity came from cinematographer Roger Deakins, who photographed the entire film and designed its fluid camera language alongside director Sam Mendes. 1917 was conceived to appear as one uninterrupted shot, demanding an extraordinary level of coordination between the camera, performers, lighting, production design and visual effects.

However, the film was not literally captured in one continuous take from beginning to end. Its 110-minute “single shot” aesthetic was constructed from numerous exceptionally long takes, with hidden transitions and visual effects used to seamlessly join them together. Deakins himself has confirmed that some of these transitions were created in post-production, while others were achieved through simpler in-camera techniques.

The Schofield Run, however, stands as one of the film’s most extraordinary examples of continuous filmmaking, a breathtaking combination of performance, choreography and Roger Deakins’ masterful cinematography.

source_details.synopsis: 1917 is a 2019 British war film directed and produced by Sam Mendes, who co-wrote it with Krysty Wilson-Cairns. It is partially inspired by stories told to Mendes by his paternal grandfather Alfred about his service during World War I. The film takes place after the German retreat to the Hindenburg Line during Operation Alberich, and follows two British soldiers in their mission to deliver an important message to call off a doomed offensive attack. The two main roles are played by George MacKay and Dean-Charles Chapman.
